newsitem.title: MEXICO: Zapatista blasts Mexico for saber-rattling.
newsitem.headline: Zapatista blasts Mexico for saber-rattling.

text.p: A Zapatista guerrilla leader on Saturday blasted the Mexican government for "sending signs of war and death" on the eve of a visit from peace mediators seeking an end to the armed conflict.

"The government doesn't want to resolve problems in a peaceful way," Commander Tacho, a top leader in the Zapatista National Liberation Army (EZLN), told a small group of journalists in his jungle hideway in southweastern Chiapas state, 120 miles (200 km) from the nearest city.
Tacho's comments came a day before Mexican legislators from a mediating commission known as Cocopa were due to arrive in Chiapas in an attempt to revive stalled peace talks.
In Buenos Aires, the Argentine magazine Noticias on Saturday quoted EZLN leader Subcommander Marcos as saying that peace between the guerrillas and the Mexican government was further than ever.
Noticias said the clandestine interview with Marcos was conducted in January but Mexican authorities seized the tape of the interview and only returned it 70 days later partially damaged.
Negotiations between the Zapatistas and the government broke down last year with each side accusing the other of holding to untenable positions.
The Zapatistas, primarily Maya Indians, want Indian autonomy but the government accuses them of seeking a separatist nation.
The armed conflict broke out on Jan. 1, 1994, when the Zaptatistas shocked the world with their existence at a time when Mexico appeared poised to enter the First World.
After about 10 days of initial fighting, the guns have fallen mostly silent, and the Zapatistas today are surrounded by the Mexican army in the jungle while a ceasefire holds.
Lately, the Zapatistas have raised concerns about violence in northern Chiapas, where land disputes have produced a series of clashes often involving government security forces.
Tacho pointed to one example in San Pedro Nixtalucum on March 14, when a clash between Tzotzil Indians and state police and the army resulted in the death of four Indians.
"They killed four brothers, leaving their children as orphans and their wives as widows," Tacho said. "This is the message this bad government sends to the Indians."
Cocopa's visit to Chiapas also seeks to quell the violence in northern Chiapas..

"As you can see, the north of the state is where there have been constant forced land evictions, but in the mountains and in the jungles as well this difficult situation has persisted the whole time we have been in the process of dialogue and negotiation," Tacho said.
